transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-15
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Sofia Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (CoralScale Lead Eng), Tom Alvarez (CoralScale Platform Ops), Priya Rao (CoralScale Security), Eli Brooks (CoralScale Product)

Summary (auto): pair-programming dev session; engineer-led demo of SDK integrations and auth; walked through Python quickstart, TS examples, and environment variables; discussed VPC/private deployment considerations and KMS for key rotation.

[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Jordan, AE, and Sofia our SE will jump into a codepair on the SDK quickstart. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: Good thanks, excited. We want to get into the actual integration so we can start a short pilot next month.
[00:18] Tom: Yeah, timeline is tight, we've got a maintenance freeze mid-december so hoping to get sandbox running this week.
[00:24] Sofia (SE): Great, we'll aim for a runnable sandbox in under an hour. I'll share the repo and run through a python quickstart and then mirror the same with TypeScript. If we hit any infra blockers we'll pause and troubleshoot.
[00:36] Priya: Quick security callout — we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs, plus SSO for the console.
[00:44] Jordan: Absolutely, we'll cover KMS hints and audit logs in the console section later. Ok Sofia, take it away.

--- Quickstart setup 
[01:02] Sofia: Alright I have a small sample app open. First step: set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env, e.g. export REDWOOD_API_KEY="rk_live_...". For CoralScale you mentioned wanting Workload Identity for GCP — you can set that up using our token exchange and the kube service account approach, but for sandbox we usually do API keys.
[01:28] Maya: Is it possible to rotate keys automatically? We want short lived tokens.
[01:34] Sofia: Yes, two options: 1) Use KMS + short-lived keys with our token service, or 2) use GCP Workload Identity Federation which issues short lived creds — depends on where you host. The SDKs handle refresh for you if you plug into the token endpoint.
[01:48] Speaker 1 (transcriber artifact): K-M-S was written as K dash M S earlier, but it's KMS.

[02:10] Sofia: I'll run the python example: pip install redwood-sdk (note: package name in repo is redwood-inference-sdk in the quickstart, some customers rename it local). Code: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate('summarize: ...') — you'll see streaming in the console.
[02:36] Maya: Can you show the streaming console? We do streaming in prod and care about backpressure.
[02:44] Sofia: Yep, here's streaming via SSE over the SDK; sample handler is in examples/streaming.py. Expect chunked JSON frames every ~200-300ms depending on batch and model. Some transcriptions earlier showed 'K V cache' but that's the KV cache for the model.

--- TypeScript parity
[03:18] Sofia: Now TS: npm i @redwood/inference ; import {Client} from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate(...). We walked through parity so both languages use the same underlying REST and websockets.
[03:38] Eli: Are there first-class types for the structured outputs? We want TS types for function-calling payloads.
[03:46] Sofia: Yes, the SDK ships types for the common responses and we've got a generated types file you can import. There are a few model-specific fields that are freeform though, so we suggest a lightweight runtime guard.

--- Auth deep-dive and KMS notes
[04:10] Priya: Regarding KMS, we need customer-managed keys and rotation policy. Can Redwood integrate with our HSM?
[04:20] Sofia: Yes — Private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations and we persist only the wrapped keys. For hosted API you can use envelope encryption with your KMS. In VPC/private deployment we have an HSM connector for on-prem. There was a slight mis-transcription in previous docs where 'H S M connector' became 'H S M connect or', sorry -- but it's supported.
[04:44] Tom: For the sandbox, we'll do API keys, but for production likely Workload Identity + KMS. How hard is the switch?
[04:52] Sofia: Minimal from SDK standpoint. The biggest work is infra — setting up token exchange and the secret rotation. We have an ops runbook; I'll share the infra checklist.

--- Console and onboarding hooks
[05:30] Jordan: Quick note: Console shows token-level usage, latency percentiles, and per-route cost breakdown. That helps you pick batching and model profiles.
[05:40] Maya: Can we create RBAC roles per team and grant only specific model access?
[05:46] Jordan: Yes, Console has SSO (SAML/SCIM) and RBAC; you can create roles and tie to projects. Audit logs include model versions and API key usage.

--- Pair-programming: run the app
[06:08] Sofia: Ok I'm going to run the python app now. (typing) Running: python examples/quickstart.py. You should see a stream with incremental tokens. 
[06:28] (shared screen)
[06:30] Sofia: There we go, tokens are streaming. Message: 'Summarize the 3 key bullet points' — you can see latency 120ms per token on this small model.
[06:42] Maya: That latency looks good. For our docs generation workload we typically see 1k-2k tokens per request; will cost be per-token as usual?
[06:50] Jordan: Yes hosted pricing is per-token generation and embeddings units. But we also have Dedicated which offers committed throughput and lower unit-cost. We'll send a pilot pricing sheet.

--- Batching, caching, and cost controls
[07:10] Sofia: Quick tips: enable prefix/KV cache for repeated prefixes, use request-level pooling for similar prompt shapes to get batching efficiency, and set a max tokens ceiling to guard cost. In the console you can enable automatic batching or manual batch sizes; we recommend starting with auto.
[07:34] Tom: Does batching increase tail latency? We need 99p latency SLOs.
[07:40] Sofia: Smart batching is workload aware; you can route low-latency traffic to small dedicated instances and lower-priority traffic to larger pooled batches. Also we have fallback policies so critical requests don't sit in a batch too long.

--- Troubleshooting and logs
[08:05] Sofia: When you see failed requests the SDK surfaces a request id which maps to the Console trace. We log model selection, kernel profile, and batch sizes in the trace so you can debug. 
[08:22] Priya: Does the trace include token-level content? Security concern.
[08:26] Sofia: By default debug traces redact sensitive prompt fields; you can configure redaction policy. For enterprise we'll set strict retention.

--- Short demo: local dev to Dedicated staging
[09:00] Sofia: Walkthrough for local dev: run docker-compose dev which spins up a local shim that proxies to sandbox; set env REDWOOD_ENV=sandbox. To transition to Dedicated staging you swap the endpoint and update policy (and for VPC you will need peering + private endpoint).
[09:26] Tom: IP allowlist and private peering — what's the typical lead time?
[09:30] Jordan: For cloud peering with our Private offering, typical lead time 2-4 days depending on your cloud team; on-prem a bit longer. For the pilot we can do internet-facing but with strict allowlist.

--- Interruptions and small misc notes (real speech artifacts)
[10:05] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) 
[10:08] Maya: sorry, quick Q — does the SDK support chunked responses for long generations so we can feed to our streaming UI?
[10:14] Sofia: Yes, that's the SSE/websocket stream we showed; it supports partial deltas and rehydration on reconnect. If you need typed deltas we can look at the function-calling structured outputs.

--- Security checklist recap
[11:02] Priya: Recap for security: 1) KMS/HSM plan for key wrapping, 2) audit logging + retention policy, 3) SAML SSO + SCIM for provisioning, 4) redaction policy for traces. Anything missing?
[11:20] Jordan: Also ensure network controls — VPC peering or private endpoints and IP allowlists. We'll include this in the infra checklist.

--- Questions about evals and quality guardrails
[12:10] Eli: For quality regression detection, can we run evals tied to prompt sets and get alerts on drift?
[12:18] Sofia: Yes, Redwood Optimize supports evals and automated regressions alerts. You can push prompt suites and get signal when outputs drop below thresholds. We'll include a sample eval runbook.

--- Pricing talk (brief)
[12:45] Jordan: Pilot pricing options: self-serve hosted tokens, or short-term Dedicated commit for predictable unit cost. We'll email the pilot pricing grid.
[12:55] Maya: For the pilot we need around 500k tokens/week estimate.
[12:59] Jordan: Ok we'll model that in the sheet.

--- Live debugging: tokenization and model choices
[13:30] Sofia: Tokenization differences can affect pricing — different open models have different tokenization density. For your large docs flows we might recommend a model with better long-context kernels and our quantized variants. There was a previous transcript where 'quantize' turned into 'quant ice' — but it's quantization profiles.
[13:58] Tom: Can we test a 16k context model for one-off runs?
[14:04] Sofia: Yes, we have 8k/16k/32k variants. For the pilot probably 16k.

--- Wrap-up and explicit next steps
[14:30] Jordan: To summarize: Sofia will share sandbox creds and the quickstart repo (py + ts) and example prompt set. Maya provides latency and prompt samples. Tom will confirm peering window and allowlist. Priya will send KMS/HSM contact info. We'll reconvene if any infra blockers pop up.
[14:54] Maya: Sounds good. One more Q: can you include an example CI job for rotating keys and updating secrets?
[15:02] Sofia: Yes, there's a CI snippet in the ops-runbook repo; I'll attach it.

Closing items (last 5 minutes were Q+A and small infra discussion).

End of transcript.

Notes: The transcript contains a few transcription artifacts (e.g., 'K V cache' for KV cache, 'quant ice' for quantize) and occasional speaker mislabels.
